author: Tumaini Carayol
description:
• Russian teen beats American 6-3, 6-4 at Indian Wells

  • French Open champion, 19, assures world No 2 ranking

The rise of Mirra Andreeva has seemed inevitable ever since she burst on to the tour as a precocious 15-year-old more than three years ago, but this week, six months after her maiden grand slam triumph at Roland Garros, she has taken another massive step forward in her career. The 19-year-old will attempt to close out the most impressive week of her career by winning one of her most significant titles after thoroughly outplaying Jessica Pegula, the fifth seed, 6-3, 6-4 to reach the championship match of the WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

A year ago, Andreeva surprisingly failed to qualify for the WTA Finals, missing out by a paltry six points after bizarrely deciding not to compete in the fin
title: Andreeva sweeps past Pegula to reach WTA Finals title match after hot-mic controversy

author: David Hytner in Madrid
description:
• Midfielder needed a break ‘to come back stronger’

  • James Trafford selected to start in goal for England

Declan Rice has admitted he had an “average” World Cup at the end of a gruelling season and needed time out during the international window in September and October in order to return stronger.

The Arsenal midfielder believes the break has served its purpose, having produced starring performances against Bayern Munich and Liverpool in recent weeks. He is now ready to hit his best level for England in Sunday’s Nations League showdown against Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium.

Continue reading...
title: Declan Rice accepts he had an ‘average World Cup’ as England gear up for Spain showdown

author: Jonathan Wilson
description:
Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago

Magnusson: And your time starts ... now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best av
title: Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson

author: Michael Hogan
description:
We’re one week away from the annual Blackpool extravaganza – but which dancers will end up at the top of the tower? Join us as we find out

Here come our hostly trio, so let’s compare their couture. Emma Willis is in a black silky two-piece with bare midriff. Josh Widdicombe is in a brown double-breast suit. Johannes Radebe has come as a Hare Krishna monk. Emma wins.

Cue clapalong titles. Which of these smiling pairs will be starved of fish and chips on Blackpool beach? Plenty of salt and vinegar for me please. And one of those little wooden forks.

Continue reading...
title: Strictly Come Dancing week eight – live

author: Raphael Rashid
description:
Filipino entry, pop and rap song Sobra-Sobra, takes 19-year-old to victory at grand final in Bangkok

Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra, to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.

Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising.

Continue reading...
title: Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia

author: Sid Lowe
description:
• England’s first game in Madrid since racist abuse in 2004

  • De la Fuente tells Tuchel ‘we’re not racists, none of us’

Luis de la Fuente has told Thomas Tuchel there is no racism in Spain after the England coach’s admission that he would remind his players of the anti-racism protocol prior to their meeting at the Metropolitano on Sunday night.

This will be the first time the countries play each other in Madrid since some of England’s black players were subjected to racist abuse in a match at the Santiago Bernabéu in 2004. And although England have returned to Spain three times without incident since then, twice in Seville and once in Alicante, Tuchel was asked about going back in the buildup to Sunday’s game. The England coach replie
title: De la Fuente adamant there is no racism in Spain despite England reminder to players

author: Robert Kitson at Allianz Stadium
description:
• England 78-15 Japan

  • Steve Borthwick’s men score 13 tries

Not every game of rugby can deliver a result for the ages. Admittedly, England do not score 13 tries every week but even if the hosts had run up 150 points they would have struggled to eclipse this weekend’s remarkable events in Cardiff and Paris. That said, in the annals of one-sided contests on this famous old stretch of turf, there have been few to match this virtual procession.

To say Japan came a distant second is to be polite in the extreme. From the moment Will Joseph collected a hat-trick of tries inside the game’s opening 20 minutes it was simply a question of how many points England would rack up and, to their credit, Maro Itoje’s side tucked into the free buffet with relish. Joseph, playing only his second Test, claimed a record-equalling five tries as his side comfortably topped their previous highest score against the Brave Blossoms.
title: Five-try Will Joseph equals record as England steamroller Japan

author: Anna Bawden
description:
Exclusive: 2,850 more patients a month would need to be treated within 62 days to meet March 2027 goal, as experts warn of failure of leadership

Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not be treated on time because the government will fail to meet its targets, amid a failure of leadership, focus and resource, experts have warned.

The NHS set an interim target to treat 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referral or consultant upgrade by March 2027. But with little more than 100 days to go, the proportion of patients starting treatment on time in September was 70.7%, down from 71.9% in August, NHS figures show.

Continue reading...
title: NHS England on track to miss key cancer treatment target by 10,000 patients

author: Marina Dunbar
description:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’ victory means Democrats will now hold 30 US governorships after midterm blowout

Democrats have captured Alaska’s governor’s seat for the first time in nearly three decades, marking another major victory for their party in a midterm election period that has dramatically shifted political power across the US.

Former Alaska state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republican opponents, including a candidate backed by Donald Trump, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998.

Continue reading...
title: Democrat wins Alaska governor’s seat for first time in nearly 30 years

author: Alex Reid
description:
• Updates from 4.40pm (GMT) start at the Allianz Stadium

  • Report: Wales stun New Zealand | Email Alex

“The overarching message this week is that we need to be alive,” said Maro Itoje – the captain and one of only three England players starting in the same position as they did against Australia.

“It’s impossible to tick off every eventuality that an opposition might do, especially a team like Japan, who have a very distinct way of playing.”

Continue reading...
title: England v Japan: Nations Championship rugby union – live

author: Damien Gayle, Graham Readfearn and Gabrielle Canon in Antalya, Turkey
description:
Civil society campaigners form protective cordon around LGBTQ+ campaigners as they unfurl flags and placards

Queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march on Saturday in the city hosting this year’s climate summit.

Turkey’s LGBTQ+ groups have faced increased persecution since September, with police targeting activists in their homes or at the offices of the NGOs that advocate for their rights.

Continue reading...
title: LGBTQ+ protesters defy crackdown in Turkey to march with Cop31 activists

author: Michael Aylwin at Principality Stadium
description:
• Wales 35-28 New Zealand

  • Home side secure first win over All Blacks since 1953

Just when you expect it the least. By what wild logic did Wales choose now to pull off a victory 73 years in the seeking? There may have been only 55,000 in Cardiff’s great stadium, but judging by the noise alone, Wales are back.

An extraordinary defensive display for the last half-hour kept wave after wave of New Zealand attacks at bay, each greeted as if the most sublime of tries by JPR, Gareth, Shane or JJ. None of those ever tasted this, but now a new generation of Welshmen, still young and hopeful, can add a win over the All Blacks to their CV.

Continue reading...
title: Wales bury 73-year All Blacks hoodoo with seismic victory over New Zealand

author: Phillip Inman
description:
Raising borrowing costs too far risks laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy

A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.

Continue reading...
title: A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and households are expected to pick up the tab

author: Anna Betts
description:
Thousands of flights still canceled as officials blamed ageing air control system for nationwide grounding

Travel chaos continued across the US on Saturday morning as airlines scrambled to recover from a four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of the flights.

On Saturday morning, more than 3,000 flights within, into or out of the US had already been canceled, according to FlightAware.

Continue reading...
title: US air travel slowly recovers from nationwide flight ground stop as chaos continues

author: Daniel Lavelle
description:
Met Office says overnight frost to give way on Saturday to ‘fine day with some sunshine’ in most regions

The UK should have a milder weekend as the unusual autumn freeze eases off, after cold health alerts were issued and temperatures plummeted overnight, forecasters have said.

After frost on Saturday morning, most of the UK should enjoy a “fine day with some sunshine”, the Met Office said. However, it will not be blue skies for everyone, as torrential rain and showers are predicted to move in from the west, bringing patchy rain and strong winds across the north and far west of the UK.

Continue reading...
title: Milder weekend forecast in UK as autumn freeze eases off

author: Tom Hunt
description:
Our coffee snob spills the beans on which granules hint at chocolate and caramel, and which leave a bitter note

• Everything you need to make great coffee

I’m a coffee snob with my own grinder, but I found the haptic thwack, whack and crack of opening the lid and film on a jar of instant coffee strangely invigorating, and rather nostalgic. When I took a deep sniff, however, disaster: all I could smell was fertiliser! Instant coffee is brewed at scorching temperatures, then either freeze-dried in a vacuum or spray-dried using hot air. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. This gives it an earthier, muskier and more bitter flavour profile, though, thankfully, with a little alchemy and hot water, those more familiar coffee aromas and flavours returned, with notes o
title: ‘All I could smell was fertiliser’: the best (and worst) supermarket instant coffee, tasted and rated

author: Phillip Inman
description:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% last month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.

Continue reading...
title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England economist says

author: Ioan Marc Jones
description:
Dylan Thomas’s Under Milk Wood reminded me of my dad’s decency and mischief. I laughed as I cried, and realised there’s no right way to go through the grieving process

I expected to break. But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him.

But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. Then, when my partner and I rearranged our bookshelves, I found the first edition of Under Milk Wood that my parents gave us on our wedding day. I turned the cover and saw the note: “And all the bells of the till
title: I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day

author: Martin Belam
description:
The first ever Eurovision Asia song contest takes place in Thailand on Saturday, and it won’t disappoint those hoping for some bizarre acts

The first ever Eurovision Asia is being held in Thailand on Saturday. The event is a more compact affair than the European version has become, and with only 11 countries competing, it isn’t a straightforward cultural import.

None of the entrants have gone near wacky Eurovision vibes such as having a singing turkey or banana-eating wolves. Restrictive attitudes to homosexuality in some of the countries where the show will be broadcast have also tempered the overt campness and LGBTQ+ representation with which Eurovision has come to be associated – there will certainly not be an equivalent of Olly Alexander getting sweaty in a grubby gym changing room.
title: Mesh masks, Nana’s lampshade and the other Beck: what to watch for at Eurovision Asia

author: Zing Tsjeng
description:
From diva-like behaviour to freebie requests that never result in a review, ‘entitled’ content creators are a growing blight on small-business owners. Now entrepreneurs are calling them out

Nicole Flanagin remembers exactly the moment an influencer came after her business. It was the early hours of a March morning and the cat cafe owner in Lenoir, North Carolina, got a message. “At 1.37,” she says, “a friend sent me the link to this girl’s TikTok.”

The 41-year-old was already having a bad 24 hours. A mother of four, Flanigan also works at a pet rescue shelter and had spent the previous day unsuccessfully fighting for a dog not to be put down. She got home exhausted and promptly conked out in bed. Then she woke up to the message.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Don’t lie to me to get free stuff’: how small businesses are fighting back against influencers

author: Jonathan Jones
description:
Van Gogh and Cézanne paintings among magnificent collection stained by allegations of abduction and killing

Twelve rarely seen masterpieces glowing with life and beauty will go on sale at Sotheby’s in New York on Wednesday.

The collection, which resembles a miniature Courtauld gallery, includes Van Gogh’s towering chestnut tree, Monet’s shimmering vista of the Tuileries and Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin, a portrait of his son in a red and black diamond-patterned costume whose angularity pushes into abstraction and must have inspired Picasso’s Harlequins.

Continue reading...
title: Masterpieces haunted by brutal past could send records tumbling at Sotheby’s

author: Madeline Horwath
description: Continue reading...
title: Madeline Horwath on the complexity of modern politics – cartoon

author: Diane Taylor
description:
Undercover ITV report also shows inadequate welfare checks at ex-military base run by firm of asylum camp billionaire Graham King

Asylum seekers accommodated at a controversial military base in East Sussex have been subjected to inadequate welfare checks, and torture survivors may have been placed there unlawfully, a new undercover documentary for ITV has revealed.

Mass accommodation sites are central to the government’s plan to end the use of hotels to house asylum seekers. For the documentary Inside The Asylum Camp, ITV’s undercover reporter got a job as a welfare officer at Crowborough and covertly filmed inside the former military training camp. The documentary claims that poor screening and welfare checks are having serious consequences for some of the asylum seekers.

Continue reading...
title: Torture survivors may have been sent to Sussex asylum camp unlawfully, documentary reveals

author: David Smith in Washington
description:
Midterm elections have defanged the US president – leaving critics to worry about his next move in his ‘fat Elvis’ stage

It was just before 3am when Donald Trump entered a crowded Manhattan ballroom, greeted by chants of “USA! USA” and theme music from the Hollywood film Air Force One. On stage, two red “Make America great again” (Maga) caps were mounted in glass cases like holy relics.

That was the scene 10 years ago this week when Trump, a businessman and reality TV star, stunned the world by beating Hillary Clinton to the White House. A decade later an unlikely president is serving an unlikely second term. But in the wake of a humiliating vote of no confidence in last week’s
title: Will Trump’s lame duck presidency push him further beyond constraints of the law?

author: Richard Luscombe
description:
US military has killed nearly 250 people in attack on ‘narco-terrorism’, and on 17 March, sank the 16 plaintiffs’ boat, leaving two with serious burns

More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen are suing the US government after they survived a military drone attack in the Pacific ocean earlier this year that sank their boat and left two of them with serious burns from the explosions.

The 17 March attack on the La Negra Francesca Duarte II was part of the Trump administration’s Operation Southern Spear campaign, announced in November 2025 ostensibly to counter “narco-terrorists” it said operated in the Caribbean and Pacific.
title: Ecuadorian fishermen who survived US boat strikes sue Trump administration

author: Guardian staff
description:
Tech company says services now restored to all customers and regions hit by one of worst IT failures in years

Microsoft has said its service is fully restored after a massive outage that caused widespread disruption to governments, businesses and public services around the world.

The technology company said on Saturday morning it had restored service to the remaining customers affected by one of the worst IT failures in years. On its Microsoft 365 status page, the US-based firm said: “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions.

Continue reading...
title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage

author: Andrew Lawrence
description:
In ambitious documentary Soul Patrol, the complicated experiences of the Vietnam war’s first Black special ops team are explored both on and off the battleground

Ask the average American to name an elite US fighting force, and they might kick off with the Rangers or the Seals. But during the Vietnam war, a specialized patrol of army volunteers became critical to the US military effort.

Known as long-range reconnaissance patrols, or LRRPs, these small teams of six to eight soldiers were dropped behind enemy lines to track supply routes and hostile positions, sometimes for days at a time. Stealth was essential. Their job was to identify targets and call in the cavalry, usually in the form of airstrikes, while avoiding direct engagement with enemy forces to preserve their cover.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I relive that mission every single day of my life’: how Black soldiers handled the Vietnam war

author: Rob Cameron in Prague
description:
Huge protest planned in Prague to oppose government’s plan to scrap licence fee, which critics say could give ministers more leverage over newsrooms

Daniel Stach was an erstwhile junior international slalom kayaker when he first walked into the headquarters of Czech Television in 2010. He had answered a Facebook ad inviting viewers to a behind-the-scenes tour of his favourite programme, a current affairs show called Hyde Park CT24. He did not expect to be offered a job shortly afterwards.

Stach, now 38, presents a science offshoot of that show doing long-form interviews. But he has also emerged as one of the most recognised public faces of the campaign to save the mandatory licence fees that fund the nation’s public broadcasters.

Continue reading...
title: Public media freedom has been eroded across central Europe. Now Czechs are rallying to protect theirs

author: Rosanna Greenstreet
description:
The author on the FBI tapping her phone, teaching herself to read aged three, and why she knits in meetings

Born in Maryland, in the US, Barbara Kingsolver, 71, won a music scholarship to DePauw University in Indiana. She became a journalist and published her first novel, The Bean Trees, in 1988. Her award-winning books include The Poisonwood Bible, The Lacuna and Demon Copperhead, which was published in 2022 and won the Pulitzer, the James Tait Black prize and the Women’s prize for fiction. In 2025, she founded the Higher Ground Women’s Recovery Residence in Lee County, Virginia, where the novel is set. Her latest novel is Partita. She lives in Virginia with her second husband and has two children.

When were you happiest?
Right after the births of my children. Those hormones are strong medicine:
title: Barbara Kingsolver: ‘What does love feel like? At 16, breaking the speed limit. Years later, a warm bath’

author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
description:
How long will it take? What challenges will they face? Series to shine light on one of biggest crises facing UK

  • ‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers

Britain is at risk of creating a lost generation. Across the country, almost a million young people – one in eight – are struggling to make the leap from school to the world of work on a lasting basis.

Before the landmark Alan Milburn review, which is expected on Tuesday, the Guardian is launching a new series to chronicle the lives of eight young people battling to get a start on the career ladder.

Continue reading...
title: Guardian to follow lives of eight young people in their search for work

author: Nicola Slawson and Jane Clinton
description:
In the first instalment of a new series, four young people reveal the impact of an endless cycle of applications and rejections

  • Guardian to follow lives of eight young people in their search for jobs

“I’ve been demoralised by the process, just constantly applying, then interviewing. I’ve just been applying to any jobs that I could find. I’d really like to be employed by now. Some companies don’t even give rejection emails … they’re not obligated to reply to the prospective interviewee, but they should be compelled to.”

Continue reading...
title: ‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers

author: Tom Holland
description:
Nearly 1,100 years ago, the nation’s first king drove out the ‘heathen’ Vikings, declared war on starvation and made ‘Englalonde’ what it is today

On 4 July, the United States celebrated its 250th birthday with all the razzmatazz and dazzle characteristic of an American public occasion. Next summer, on 12 July, England will be celebrating the 1,100th anniversary of the event that, more than any other, marked the founding of the country – but of razzmatazz and dazzle there will be, I suspect, very little.

The great turning point took place on 12 July 927, beside the river Eamont in what today is Cumbria. Here, amid an untamed wilderness of mountains and lakes, the most powerful king in Britain had summoned other kings and lords from across the island to meet him for a summit.

Continue reading...
title: King Æthelstan founded England in the year 927. Why don’t we celebrate that anniversary? | Tom Holland

author: Caroline Davies
description:
Charles marks 78th birthday and 50th anniversary of King’s Trust charity with a playlist for special episode of podcast

King Charles marked his 78th birthday on Saturday joking with Elton John that they were “still standing” as he appeared on the singer-songwriter’s Rocket Hour for a shared musical journey.

In a special recorded episode of the Apple Radio show to mark the 50th anniversary of the monarch’s charity the King’s Trust, Charles’s playlist included John’s I’m Still Standing.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Still standing’: king jokes as he appears on Elton John’s Rocket Hour

author: Molly Oldfield
description:
Five multiple-choice questions – set by children – to test your knowledge, and a chance to submit your own junior brainteasers for future quizzes

  • ​Submit a question

Molly Oldfield hosts Everything Under the Sun, a podcast answering children’s questions. Do check out her books, Everything Under the Sun and Everything Under the Sun: Quiz Book, as well as her new title, Everything Under the Sun: All Around the World.

title: Why do whales need to live in the sea when they breathe air? The kids’ quiz

author: Miguel Dantas
description:
The captain, the talisman, the brand: former teammates and experts discuss Portugal entering a new era after 23 years

There are days football fans hope will never come. For Portugal, this is one of them. For 23 years, Cristiano Ronaldo has been more than the country’s greatest footballer; he has been its defining sporting figure, a symbol of national pride and constant presence in the lives of supporters. After 234 appearances and 146 goals, the No 7 brought that chapter to a close and on Saturday night the team will play their first game without him.

The national side are losing more than a great footballer; they are also losing one of the world’s biggest brands. Daniel Sá, the executive director of the Portuguese institute of marketing administration, believes Portugal require reinvention to attract at least some of the millions of viewers who tuned in becau
title: Portugal did the extraordinary with Cristiano Ronaldo. Can they do it without him?

author: Jacqui Housden
description:
The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden

  • Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

If you’ve spent any time looking at the big headlines this week then you’ll know it’s high time for a good old break from the news. Take a breath, and bliss out with some long reads (mostly) a long way away from the doom cycle.

Continue reading...
title: Five Great Reads: Sleep paralysis, parakeets and problematic laundry

author: Phil Harrison, Priya Elan, Ali Catterall, Alexi Duggins and Simon Wardell
description:
This Berlin-set origin story stars Ann Skelly and Rory Kinnear. Plus: the clever, creepy mystery of Yaga takes another turn. Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, BBC One
If you ever wondered how Fiona Shaw’s Killing Eve MI6 oddball Carolyn Martens got so eccentric, you’re in luck. This drama, set in East Berlin in 1982, is her origin story: Martha/Carolyn (Ann Skelly) is a bored junior spy when Rory Kinnear’s agent Graham Anderson gives her an assignment that leads her into a menage a trois with a CIA operative and a Stasi officer. It doesn’t quite manage the irreverent mischief of prime Killing Eve but it’s still spicy fun. Phil Harrison

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: a spicy, funny cold war Killing Eve prequel

author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
description:
The imprisonment of Russell Brand and allegations against David Walliams have prompted scrutiny of a culture that encouraged male transgression

In a 2008 episode of BBC Two’s comedy panel show Never Mind the Buzzcocks, the choreographer Arlene Phillips – the only woman on the programme – was told by the host Simon Amstell: “You look like you run a good whore house.” In reply, Phillips told a story with what appeared to be faux sincerity: while working with big stars, she explained, she would sometimes be asked to find dancers with “very special abilities” who might want to party after filming. Another panellist, the TV presenter Dermot O’Leary, mimed picking up a phone and said: “When you’re dancing tonight, do you mind having sex afterwards?” Everyone laughed.

Russell Brand’s
title: Is it finally OK to be frank about 2000s pop culture? ‘It was profoundly, cheerfully horrible to women’

author: Guardian Staff
description:
We’ve unboxed, nibbled and played with hundreds of gifts to find the perfect present for everyone – from cheery stocking fillers and feelgood treats to Jude Bellingham’s favourite game

Filled with dread about Christmas shopping? Luckily for you, we’ve had a head start and spent the whole year playing, tasting, sipping, sniffing and putting hundreds of items to the test to help you find the best Christmas gifts for everyone on your list.

We’ve recruited experts, from three-year-old toy testers to gardening gurus, beauty connoisseurs to our own team here on the Filter, to bring you tried-and-tested recommendations we know will bring joy this Christmas and beyond. From bloody marys and sleep masks to mushroom-growing kits and taste-test-winning biscuits, here are 369 carefully curated gift ideas to suit even the fussiest recipients. Merry Christmas!

Continue reading...
title: 369 best Christmas gifts for 2026 – tried, tested and loved by the Filter UK

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve are in a custody battle in Cristian Mungiu’s powerful drama, while the Irish stadium monsters are back, and back on form, after nine years away

Fjord
Out now
Romanian auteur Cristian Mungiu’s latest stars Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve in a Norway-set drama about a Romanian couple whose five children are taken from them by the state. Based on real events, it looks at how an intersection of immigrant status, religious beliefs and prejudice may have contributed to the separation.

Continue reading...
title: From Fjord to U2: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

author: Jackson Boxer
description:
A rich, comforting plateful of sweet, crunchy hispi topped with a cheesy cream – like a bowl of pasta, only without the carbs

This is a fun recipe that takes advantage of the hispi cabbage’s sweet nature and pliant structure. You can give it a really hard blast of heat, and it will crisp, caramelise and smoke, but still retain a lot of its easy freshness and bright crunch; it will also take on a pleasing, slightly slippery texture, like buttered noodles. This plate has the satisfaction of a hearty bowl of pasta without being nearly so enervating, and it works fantastically as a side dish, too, either as a companion to toasted whole grains or some grilled mushrooms.

Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowl
title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for sauteed cabbage with cheese cream and sunflower seeds

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Lucy, 40, a general manager, meets Leon, 45, an operations manager at a food charity

What were you hoping for?
I’m a regular reader and have always wanted to be in the column, so mostly here for the vibes. Bumping into the love of my life would be nice, though …

Continue reading...
title: Blind date: ‘Would we meet again? We’ve swapped numbers … ’

author: Calum Jacobs
description:
The arguments have been endless and they are fatuous. Wales and Scotland stopped conflating national identity with race: why can’t England?

In 2021, the then shadow justice secretary, David Lammy, asserted his Englishness on the Saturday LBC programme he hosted, only for a caller named Jean to insist that his African-Caribbean heritage disqualified him. He could be British, she maintained, but “never be English”. Jean defended Englishness as though it were a possession she would never surrender to the country’s Black populace. Lammy’s entreaties to recognise it as a civic identity were ignored, as Jean attempted to demarcate its racial boundary live, on air.

After cross-party condemnation of Jean’s nativi
title: It’s absurd that ‘Black English’ is not on the census. We should be free to claim that identity if we choose | Calum Jacobs

author: Sandra Laville
description:
This week the Soil Association withdrew certification from organic salmon after 20 years. What went wrong?

The first haul of farmed salmon in Britain was a relatively modest 14 tonnes, produced off the west coast of Scotland near Fort William in 1971.

For Unilever, the vast multinational that pioneered salmon farming, it was a triumph after years of experimenting with how to cage fish, battle against diseases and cope with the wild weather. Unilever had spotted in the 1960s that farming salmon, which until then was caught wild and remained a relative luxury, would create a mass market, lower costs and provide steady profits. By 1976, it had expanded into three Scottish sites producing 116 tonnes of fish each year.

Continue reading...

author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi

The first drone struck the busy transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab as hundreds of people gathered to board trucks to take them back to their homes.

Ten minutes later on the evening of 18 October, a second drone hit the same site in the town in West Kordofan state, Sudan. At least 139 people were killed.

author: Doc Rowe
description:
Ryton-on-Dunsmore, Warwickshire: It takes place in the dark, and this year there’s misty rain to contend with, but the wroth silver ceremony has endured for centuries

Before sunrise on 11 November, while most people are still sleeping, representatives of 25 Warwickshire parishes gather on Knightlow Hill to observe one of Britain’s oldest surviving customs.

The wroth silver ceremony is at least 850 years old, first appearing in written records in 1170, and requires payment of annual rent to the landowner, the Duke of Buccleuch. Despite misty rain this year, more than 60 people attend amid the noise of traffic from the A45.

Continue reading...
title: Country diary: One of Britain’s oldest surviving traditions – and it’s all over in four minutes | Doc Rowe

author: Anna Moore
description:
In 2016, Mariah Rief, then 19, thought she was going to a modelling job at a hotel. Once there, she was sex trafficked. She knows of 15 fellow victims who have since died by suicide or drug overdose – and is determined to stop it ever happening again

When people ask Mariah Rief about her experience as a survivor of sex trafficking, they tend to start with the Craigslist ad which led the then 19-year-old to a “modelling shoot” at the Hilton hotel in San Diego. For others, the story starts when Rief enters the lobby and meets Theodore Gyi, the “photographer”. Or after they’ve taken the elevator up to a room, Rief standing at the threshold, Gyi behind her blocking her exit – and just inside the door, the silhouette of a second man waiting.

title: How I survived being forced into pornography: ‘I died in that hotel room. I was a walking corpse’

author: Sophie Heawood
description:
After years of celebrity interviews, I have learned not to be fooled by the allure of fame. We never really know them – we know what they want us to know

As I sat in Southwark crown court, listening to the final day of Russell Brand’s trial, there was one subject that came up repeatedly, invoked as often by his defence as the prosecution. I don’t mean sex or coercion, but fame. It ran through every victim impact statement and loomed so large in the courtroom that it felt as if it was almost on trial itself.

I’m an entertainment journalist who has been covering celebrities for more than 20 years – as long as Brand has been one – and I have written about him at various stages of his career. But I went to Southwark crown court as a member of the public who wanted to see justice done. For the women he had hurt, for the ones who couldn’t get as far as the courtroom, and for all of us who came of age at a time when rape culture was so fast and furious that young women mistook
title: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood

author: Amelia Gentleman
description:
One was a high-profile defendant watched by more than 100 journalists. Another was an unknown man who preyed on a girl almost half his age. Their stories played out minutes apart, one entirely out of the spotlight

What is going on inside Russell Brand’s head as he arrives at court for the start of his rape trial? He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.”

He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God.
title: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?
